extracted.intended_audience: readers of poetry and occasional public speakers (those asked to give toasts/dinner speeches)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short, light, effective after-dinner toasts or impromptu dinner speeches—the ephemeral, entertaining sort suitable for commencement or social gatherings. Emphasizes tone, length, and common anti-patterns to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a good dinner speech / toast
rubrics_metrics.description: A toast or after-dinner speech should be light, airy, and adapted to the occasion—brief, graceful, and more like 'winged prose' than full poetry or heavy discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key guidance and examples from the text: 'I've a notion, I think, of a good dinner speech, / Tripping light as a sandpiper over the beach,'; 'Not poetry,--no, not quite that, but as good, / A kind of winged prose that could fly if it would.' A toast should be 'Light, airy, and free, / The foam-Aphrodite of Bacchus's sea, / A fancy-tinged bubble, an orbed rainbow-stain, / That floats for an instant 'twixt goblet and brain.' Avoid heavy, moralizing or long-winded speeches—anti-patterns include speeches that 'start with a pop, / Then wander and maunder, too feeble to stop,' or those that attempt weighty argument at a dinner: 'When I hear your set speeches that start with a pop, / Then wander and maunder... I--well, I sit still, and my sentiments smother.' The speaker should aim for ephemeral charm: a 'breath-born perfection, half something, half naught, / And breaks if it strike the hard edge of a thought.' Practical notes: be brief, favor light fancy and surprise, avoid 'manoeuvring the heavy dragoons of the mind,' and strive to leave 'on memory's rim just a sense / Something graceful had gone by.'
